For an infinite set $A$ of positive integers and an integer $b\ge2$, write
\[
 X_A(b)=\sum_{a\in A}\frac1{b^a-1}.
\]
The question is when a condition on the exponents forces this number, and the corresponding sum over every infinite subset of~$A$, to be irrational.

The distinction from the reciprocal-summability criterion is visible in the source paper's example
\[
 A_\star=\{2^km:k\ge1,\ m\text{ odd},\ 1\le m\le2^{2^k}\},\qquad P=\{2\}.
\]
Within the layer $v_2(a)=k$, reciprocal summation discounts each odd $m$ by $2^{-k}$; weighted summation discounts it by $(2^{2^k}-1)^{-1}$.

sentences.text: To compare the layers, put $S_r=\sum_{1\le m\le2^r,\ m\ \mathrm{odd}}1/m$. Grouping the odd integers into intervals $[2^j,2^{j+1})$ gives $r/4\le S_r\le r$ for integers $r\ge2$.

The reciprocal contribution of each disjoint layer is at least $2^{-k}S_{2^k}\ge1/4$. Its weighted contribution satisfies
\[
 \frac{S_{2^k}}{2^{2^k}-1}\le\frac{2^k}{2^{2^k}-1}\le2^{1-k},
\]
so the layer contributions have a convergent geometric majorant in the weighted sum.

sentences.text:
To see why both averages can be made small, let $p_*=\max P$, take $L$ divisible by~$F$, and, for $H\ge2p_*$, set
\[
 Q=L\prod_{p\in P}p^{\lfloor\log_p H\rfloor},\qquad
 G=\lfloor H/p_*\rfloor,\qquad M=\lfloor b^{G/2}\rfloor.
\]
If $h_P(a)\le H$, then $h_P(a)\mid Q$; otherwise $\gcd(a,Q)\ge G$. Thus the small-$h_P(a)$ terms are controlled by the weighted sum and~\eqref{eq:worked-dyadic}, while the large-$h_P(a)$ terms gain a denominator $b^G-1$. With $F$ and its common multiple $L$ fixed, $Q\le LH^{|P|}$, whereas $M$ grows exponentially in~$H$. Consequently $Q/M\to0$ and $GM/b^G\to0$. The finite mean is bounded by $\varepsilon$ plus terms tending to zero; the exponents $a>QT$ contribute at most $4/T$. These are the two scale choices in the source proof~\cite[Section~2]{paper257}.

Since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, one of the displacements is smaller than $1/q$, a contradiction. Passing to an infinite $B\subseteq A$ only decreases the weighted sum, and $b^{h_P(a)}-1\ge2^{h_P(a)}-1$ gives the all-base conclusion from the binary hypothesis~\cite[Section~2]{paper257}.
sentences.warrant: Explains the exact displacement identity, positivity, common modulus and two-scale averaging in the existing proof; this exposition is not a newly checked Lean proof or a claim to omit the weighted hypothesis.
